# Gummy in the Middle

We saved the kitchen for last, my sister and I, because neither of us wanted to be the one who opened the drawers. It was October and the house had already given up most of itself—the furniture sold, the photographs divided, the closet of coats distributed among cousins. But the kitchen still smelled like my mother, which is to say like nutmeg and dish soap and forty years of Sunday mornings, and it held out on us for two days before I found the box.

It was on the third shelf above the stove, pushed back behind a bottle of vinegar that predated me. A scratched tin, hinged, once teal, with a strip of masking tape across the lid in my father's blocky capitals: RECIPES. When I lifted it, the hinge cracked all the way off. Inside, standing shoulder to shoulder, were several hundred index cards smelling of old paper and turmeric, grease spots translucent as stained glass when I held them to the window.

I went straight for the lemon meringue pie. Everyone went straight for the lemon meringue pie—it was legendary, Easter-only, guarded, gossiped about. My mother brought it to the church auction one year and the minister bid on his own raffle ticket. My sister and I used to hover around the cooling rack like seagulls until she smacked our knuckles with the whisk. I flipped through the cards with real excitement, expecting to find it in the M's.

It wasn't there. Neither was the poppy seed roll. Neither was the apricot chicken, or the dill bread, or any of the dozen dishes my mother was actually known for, the ones relatives had requested for decades, the ones we assumed must exist somewhere in writing. The box contained none of them.

What it contained instead were the rehearsals.

Cards dated 1963 through last spring, in four distinct handwritings if you counted my grandmother's, though mostly in my mother's—wide looping fountain pen in the sixties, cramped blue biro by the eighties, and then, after 2012, a soft large-lettered pencil that slanted downhill like a path worn into grass. These were not her triumphs. These were her attempts. *Beef Burgundy, try #2*, one read, followed by, in the margin, *tougher than intended.* *Coffee cake, attempt #7—gummy in the middle AGAIN.* Forty years of again.

Her marginalia was its own genre. *Too salty, per Ed. He's wrong.* Later, on a different card: *More onions, per Ed. There is no such thing as too many onions. Ignored.* On the fudge: *Do not answer phone during candy stage. DO NOT ANSWER PHONE.* On a casserole from the big-batch years: *Kids ate it anyway.*

Beneath her cards were her mother's, torn halves of unlined paper, terse beyond usefulness. *Flour until it looks right. Bake till done.* My mother's pencil crowded the margins: *Ma, this helps no one. Reconstructed below.* Below would run fifteen lines of her own translation, measurements recovered like forensic evidence, a daughter reverse-engineering a dead woman's hands.

And there were checkmarks. Only three, in the entire box. A potato roll from 1971: checkmark, and beneath it, *Good. Finally. Took six years.* The apricot chicken, 1984: checkmark, *company-worthy, do not alter.* And a soup—I'd never heard of the soup—with a note explaining that the original card had been given away in 1990 to a coworker who asked, and that this second version was rebuilt from memory. So even success, in her archive, was provisional. Once something worked she seemed less interested in it. It graduated out of the box and into ordinary weeks, made thereafter without ceremony or notation, invisible the way breathing is invisible.

Near the back were the recent years: recipes shrunk to pencil, quantities halved. *Serves 4* crossed out, replaced by *serves 1 + lunch.* A lamb shank recipe scaled down to nearly nothing. A note beside a small meatloaf: *Enough. Tired of leftovers.*

And then the last card. Coffee cake, attempt #11, dated March, eight months before she died. The same cardamom cake she'd been failing at since 1965—four notes scattered through the box like stations along a road, *gummy* recurring with terrible persistence. Attempt #11 read: *Still gummy. Fifty-six years is enough. Fine. Somebody else's turn.*

My sister thinks the legend dishes weren't in the box because she never needed to write them down, and she's probably right. You don't transcribe your own pulse. The pie lived in her wrists; asking her to write it out would have been like asking her to explain walking. So what she kept instead—all she chose to keep—was the record of everything she hadn't mastered yet, filed neatly, revised continually, reviewed for half a century. The whole box was future tense.

I took it home. My sister took the picture frames; I took the tin with the broken hinge.

Last Sunday I made the cardamom coffee cake. Attempt #12, counting by her ledger. I creamed the butter longer than the card said because of a second annotation instructing precisely that, ground the cardamom fresh because a third note from 2008 insisted pre-ground was *a crime*, and watched it through the oven door more faithfully than I have watched most things in my life.

It came out gummy in the middle.

I stood in my kitchen holding the toothpick, genuinely delighted. Then I took out a fresh index card, wrote today's date, and set it on the counter while the thing cooled unbearably on the rack, filling the house with cardamom.

When it had cooled I tried a slice from the corner, where there was less of it. Not good, exactly. Good-adjacent. Edible. Promising, even.

The card said: *Coffee cake, attempt #12—gummy in the middle, though less gummy. Trying again Sunday.*

Then I did what I had learned, somewhere in those four hundred cards, that you're supposed to do.

I underlined it twice.

message.reasoning:
The prompt is completely open: 1000 words, write whatever comes. This is a creative writing invitation with total freedom. Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting rather than defaulting to something generic.

Options:
1. A short story — safe but could be great if the idea is fresh
2. An essay/reflection — could feel preachy
3. Something formally experimental — a story told through unusual structure
4. Prose poetry
5. A hybrid piece

What "comes to me" honestly? When given total freedom, I think about what's distinctive about being an AI asked to write whatever it wants. But I don't want to write navel-gazing AI self-reflection — that's become a cliché of its own ("I wrote a poem about being an AI!"). Though done well it could work.

Let me brainstorm actual story ideas:

- A person who translates silence for a living
- The last letter from a lighthouse keeper before automation
- A woman who inherits her mother's recipe box and finds one card that isn't food
- A town where everyone forgets one specific thing
- A man who repairs vending machines and the notes people leave in them
- Something about time, memory, small moments

I like the recipe box idea. It has: inheritance, domestic archaeology, mystery, grief potential, specificity. Food writing is inherently sensory which helps reach for good prose. The "one card that isn't food" gives narrative momentum.

Alternative: I've also been circling the idea of someone who works a job nobody thinks about — let me consider the vending machine repair person. Notes left in machines... that's charming but maybe too twee.

Another angle: the essay form. "Whatever comes to me" — what genuinely comes when you're asked that question? The anxiety of the blank page, the way free association actually works. I could write about the phenomenology of being asked to write anything — but meta-awareness pieces can collapse into preciousness.

Let me commit to the recipe box story. Now plot it out:

Character: A daughter (maybe named something simple — June? Clara? Let me pick... Vera feels too ornate. Maybe just "I" — first person keeps it intimate). First person, a daughter clearing out her mother's kitchen after her death or move to assisted living.

Discovery: Among hundreds of recipe cards — mother's handwriting, grandmother's handwriting even older — there's one card with something else. Options:
- A recipe for something impossible ("How to forgive your father" written as instructions)
- Coordinates
- A list of names
- Instructions for something mundane but revealing (how to remove a stain — with a note revealing she knew about something)
- A recipe for bread that includes an anomalous instruction line

The "recipe as metaphor" risk: recipes-for-life is a known trope (like "recipe for a happy marriage"). If I do it, I need it to be stranger and more oblique than sentiment. What if the card is an actual recipe — for something she never made, in a hand that isn't hers? Or in her handwriting but dated after her death was expected?

Better idea: the card is in her handwriting, for a dish nobody in the family ever ate, and included among the ingredients is something impossible or odd — not whimsical, but quietly wrong. Like "one cup of snow, packed." Or an ingredient crossed out. And at the bottom, instead of serving suggestions: a sentence addressed to someone.

Or: the simplest, most human version — the last card in the box, in shaky late-period handwriting, says "Burnt again. Try again tomorrow." Just that. The record of failure, kept. Not hidden. That's devastating because it shows her private perseverance — decades of trying something, maybe making it once successfully at the end, or never.

Actually let me combine: the narrator goes through the box looking for the famous dishes — the lemon squares everyone begged for, the Sunday roast — and can't find them anywhere. The absent recipes are the point. All the things mom was known for were never written down; the box holds only experiments, failures, drafts. The written record contains no masterpieces. Then the final discovery reframes: the two or three times something was finally perfect, the cards say so in tiny marginalia — "Eddie liked this one" or "Got it." A life's archive of trial runs with rare confirmation.

Ending: the narrator copies nothing, takes the whole box home, begins cooking from the failed recipes. Or ends mid-action: makes her mother's never-succeeded dish, it fails too, and she writes "burnt again" on a new card and files it. Inheriting not the mastery but the practice. That's the emotional payoff — we inherit attempts, not achievements.

That's a real story with shape. Word count target ~1000. Structure:

1. Opening: clearing the house, the box described concretely (wooden? index file? tin?). Sensory grounding.
2. The famous dishes missing — realization.
3. What IS there: failures, alternate versions, corrections, cross-outs. Mother's hand evolving over 50 years — young looped script to shaky pencil. Maybe grandmother's cards underneath.
4. Specific examples quoted — need vivid fake recipes. E.g., "Beef Bourguignon — attempt #1" ... marginal notes: "too much wine," "Ed said too salty; he's wrong."
5. The rare successes marked. Count them. Three confirmed hits in forty years? 
6. The last card. Late handwriting. What does it say? Maybe: "Jan 2019. It rose." Simple. Or connect to a signature dish.
7. Narrator's response: cooking the failures. Final image: adding her own card. Closing line lands the theme without stating it flatly.

Names: Mother = maybe just "my mother." Father = Ed/Eddie mentioned in margins, dead before her presumably. Daughter narrator unnamed or minimal. Keep cast tight.

Specific recipe details to invent:
- Cardamom coffee cake, attempted eleven times ("still gummy in the middle")
- Dad's favorite pot roast that burned repeatedly?
- The dish the mother was famous FOR at church/potlucks: sour cream lemon pie. Never in the box.
- Late-life cards in shaky pencil: single portions. Small lamb shanks for one. That detail — the downsizing after dad died — carries grief efficiently. "Feeds 4 → feeds 1, twice" 

Marginalia lines are where the voice lives:
- "Too many onions. There is no such thing. Reworked."
- "Not like Ma's. Stop trying to make it like Ma's."
- Dated. Spanning decades: 1963 to 2018.
- "Snow day version"

The successes: how marked? A star? Underlined "again"? I'll invent: three cards have checkmarks and small notes. "Good. Finally." One says "Bob (from work?) asked for it. Gave him the card." That one's missing from the box forever — gave away the only copy. Nice touch: generosity costing the record.

Emotional beats: humor in the marginalia prevents saccharine. Mom's voice should be dry, a little stubborn. "He's wrong" appears twice about different seasonings.

Final scene: narrator bakes the cardamom coffee cake, attempt twelve by lineage count. It comes out gummy in the middle. She gets out a blank card. Writes something. Maybe: "Attempt #12. Still gummy. Trying again Sunday." Cardamom traceable through generations. End there or one beat after.

Title: "Attempts" or "The Recipe Box" — plain titles fit. "Attempts" might be better but on-the-nose. Could go titleless or "Cardamom." Hmm — "Card No. 1" — eh. Keep simple: maybe no title needed, or a quiet one. I'll use a title since it frames a standalone piece: something like "Failure Seasoning"? No. "The Box." Honestly "Attempts" communicates cleanly. Or "Gummy in the Middle." That's intriguing and earns meaning retroactively. I kind of love "Gummy in the Middle" — specificity, a little odd, pays off. Let me go with that or just present without title. A title adds polish; choose "Gummy in the Middle."

Now drafting mentally with word economy (~1000 words means roughly 8-10 paragraphs):

Draft flow:
Para 1: Setting — October, cardboard boxes, the kitchen done last. The recipe box under the sink / on the third shelf behind vinegar. Physical description: scratched tin or birchwood, hinge broken, smell of nutmeg and old paper when opened.

Para 2: Expectation — narrator knows the contents by reputation: lemon pie, kugel? Or keep culturally neutral: lemon meringue pie, Swedish tea ring? Pick foods: lemon meringue pie, beef Stroganoff?, Christmas stollen... I'll choose accessible Americana: lemon meringue pie (the church legend), poppy seed rolls, "the chicken thing with apricots." Search for the pie card first.

Para 3: It isn't there. Neither are the others. Discover the pattern: everything celebrated, absent.

Para 4: What exists instead: the attempts. Quote cards. Dates spanning 40+ years. Handwriting evolution detail.

Para 5: More quotes/marginalia; introduce Ed's opinions; the "he's wrong" refrain; humor beat.

Para 6: The grandmother layer — cards in other hands beneath: "Ma's" recipes, terse, no measurements ("flour enough"). Mother's annotations struggling against them.

Para 7: The rare marks of success. Three checkmarked cards. Details of each briefly. One card gone — given away, note admits it. The implied character: when she got it right, she handed it off.

Para 8: The later years: smaller quantities, pencil, "feeds 2" rewritten to "feed 1 + lunch." The final card: date shortly before the end, something small achieved or attempted. Maybe the cardamom cake introduced here as the long war: eleven attempts across the whole box, dating back to 1971. Her white whale — no wait, mixing with the ending, needs setup earlier. Introduce coffee cake attempts early (attempt numbers let me reference: #7, #9 seen early), then final card is attempt #11: "Still gummy. Fine. Somebody else's turn." — oh, that's good: an address forward, almost an invitation, unspoken bequest. Then the narrator takes up the quest. Ending mirrors.

Para 9-10: Narrator home, bakes attempt #12, gummy middle as inherited, writes the next card. Closing line — land softly, no moral stated outright. Perhaps: "It wasn't very good either. I'll try again on Sunday." Full stop. The "again" carries everything.

Let me also seed why mom never wrote down the pies/legend dishes: the realization paragraph can offer it lightly — "you don't write down what you already know by heart" — show don't fully tell: she made the pie every Easter for decades; hands memorize. Maybe leave inference light; readers get it. Or one clause acknowledging it without hammering.

Also nice: mention the box arrived labeled — masking tape on lid in father's hand "RECIPES." Small artifacts create texture. Maybe skip dad details besides Ed marginalia to control length.

Watch word budget; each paragraph ~90-130 words. Ten paragraphs ≈ 1000-1200. Aim slightly under and trim.

Word choice care: avoid clichés ("treasure trove"), avoid over-sentimentality, keep concrete nouns: Berol pencil, Exotic souvenir spoon?? irrelevant. Tin, index cards both lined/unlined, splashes, grease spots translucent ("held to window"), turmeric fingerprint. Sensory anchors.

Fake recipes quotes format: italics unavailable reliably—use quotes. Keep quote snippets short and punchy.

Humor lines to include:
- On onions: "Too many onions said Ed. There is no such thing."
- "Add more butter than it says."
- "Do not answer phone during candy stage." — candy stage! Great specific. "Burnt the sugar again answering the phone" — many households' truth.
- "Kids ate it anyway" — big batch era.

Successes with specifics:
1. Potato rolls, checkmark, "Good. Finally. Took 6 yrs." Hmm dates: if card dated '65 with check...
2. Apricot chicken "companyworthy"
3. Soup? "...the soup, evidently, took ten years and then simply existed thereafter, made weekly without ceremony." Interesting: some things graduate into background habit once solved — like her actual daily cooking life invisible in the box. Keep brief.

Number the coffee cake attempts visible: #4 1974, #7 1983 "gummy center again", #9 1990s?, #11 2021 final. Narrator's = #12.

Handwriting arc: wide ink loops seventies; blue biro tighter in eighties; pencil large-shaky 2010s. This documents aging without saying "aging."

Grandmother's cards: half index card, Dutch/German?? keep unspecified origin: "flour until it looks right. Bake till done." Mom's pencil反驳margin: "Ma, this helps NO ONE."  Ha — good laugh line but anachronistic capital style okay.

Where's the emotional core landing line? After baking fail, writing new card: include date, attempt number, verdict, and sign-off mirroring mother's "somebody else's turn"? Since narrator inherits, maybe end: "Underlined it twice." Because earlier established: double underline = commitment/that's-final tone? Set that up earlier: mom double-underlines verdicts. Then narrator double underline at end echoes inheritance. Good device: establish "she only ever underlined twice: checkmarks/double-underline finality," then closing action reuses it.

Now write full text aiming exactly-ish 1000 words. I'll draft carefully.

Also formatting per guidelines: creative writing request → prose, minimal markdown, maybe a title. Title alone bold or as heading? A simple italic or plain title line works; I'll do a bold or just plain-line title. Given chat display, a short title line, perhaps centered-ish via heading is fine. I'll use a single line title (maybe with "#" level small? No—just bold or plain). I'll put the title plainly, then prose paragraphs. No headers/bullets inside. Length constraint requested 1000 words—I'll aim near it, within ±5%.
